Chicago (Associated Press) — A U.S. immigration judge ruled Wednesday that the Palestinian American leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque can be deported on grounds his presence harms U.S. foreign policy, while dismissing allegations he lied on his green card application.

Salah Sarsour was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in March in Milwaukee. A federal judge in June ordered Sarsour released, saying he had raised "substantial credible" claims that the Trump administration was targeting him for his public criticism of Israel and his advocacy for Palestinian rights.

Sarsour said in a statement that the ruling was "deeply disappointing," but that he plans to appeal.

"I will continue to fight for my freedom of speech and my right to remain in this country that I have called home for over 30 years," Sarsour said.

The government argued Sarsour's decades-old terrorism conviction in Israel made him a threat to U.S. national security and accused him of hiding that fact on his green card application.

Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi sided with the government, but dismissed claims he had lied.

Sarsour said he feared for his life if deported to the West Bank.

Sarsour was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and was imprisoned in Israel in 1988, when he acknowledged throwing Molotov cocktails and stones at Israeli soldiers. In 1995, he was also convicted of attempted possession of weapons and ammunition. Sarsour denies committing the acts. His legal team says he was tortured and forced to confess in both cases.

Sarsour has no criminal record in the U.S. and has lived in the country since 1993. His lawyers say the U.S. government has known about his Israeli convictions since he arrived. He is president of the Milwaukee Muslim Society.

Being deported to the West Bank would mean "the end of my life," Sarsour said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday.

If Sarsour is deported, his treatment at the hands of Israeli authorities in the past is "likely a good indication of what he will face," one of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, told The Associated Press.

Lawyers say Sarsour will fight the deportation order

Taurel said Wednesday that Sarsour is being unfairly targeted.

"If Salah can be deported for his speech supporting Palestinian human rights, then anyone can face the same fate," Taurel said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued an unusual memo in June 2025 saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi. Both Khalil and Mahdawi are Palestinian rights advocates whom the Trump administration has tried to deport. That's according to court documents.

Ahead of the judge's ruling, Taurel said Sarsour would fight the deportation and likely need to prove he would face torture if deported to Israel.

"It's a high bar, although I think we can meet it in this case — given Salah's past experiences, and how the Israeli government has treated people in his situation," Taurel said.

Sarsour was scheduled to appear in court for a status hearing on Wednesday.

Sarsour says he was tortured and forced to confess

Jawad Boulos defended Sarsour in Israel and represented him when he was convicted. Boulos testified in August that Sarsour had been coerced into confessing and was never convicted of any charge involving a terrorist organization.

Sarsour's brother, Mohammad Sarsour, testified in July that his brother was dirty, gaunt, and had lost significant weight when he appeared in an Israeli court, and complained of pain. Boulos also testified that Sarsour was tortured while held by Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency. The Department of Homeland Security pressed Boulos on his torture allegations, asking how he knew they were true.

Sarsour's current defense team has questioned why U.S. authorities waited until this year to arrest him. Taurel said the government has known for decades about Sarsour's time in Israeli prison, and Sarsour never hid the information from U.S. immigration authorities.

Experts on coerced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails also testified on Sarsour's behalf. Israeli military courts have repeatedly been scrutinized for alleged lack of due process and high conviction rates among Palestinians. Israel denies the allegations.

U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from ICE custody in June while his immigration case proceeded. Hanlon found Sarsour likely had arguments that the U.S. government was retaliating against him in violation of his free speech rights, and that attorneys representing ICE and DHS had failed to explain why he had suddenly been deemed a threat after living legally in the country for decades.

The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon's decision to release Sarsour from ICE custody.

Sarsour has Type 2 diabetes and his lawyers say he lost more than 30 pounds (about 14 kilograms) while in ICE custody, where his blood sugar levels were measured only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death.

An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits over similar allegations of medical neglect.

Sarsour is among several people in the United States who have been detained and threatened with deportation since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023 for publicly supporting Palestinians.

Mayes-Osterman is a member of the AP/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
